file: papers/pdf/Lane et al - 2020 - Engineering Serendipity - When Does Knowledge Sharing Lead to Knowledge Production.pdf
about: A field experiment at a medical research symposium testing how field and intellectual similarity between scientists shape whether engineered serendipitous face-to-face encounters lead to knowledge transfer, collaboration (copublication) and citation over six years.

candidates.label: Chance encounter with unmet people
candidates.definition: A serendipitous encounter exposes a person to people they would not otherwise have met and to unfamiliar information that can be combined with their own knowledge.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes meeting someone by chance (e.g., happening to attend the same talk or event) who the person would not otherwise have met, and encountering new information from them.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The meeting was deliberately sought out with a known, targeted partner; that is planned search, not a chance encounter.

candidates.label: Engineered serendipity
candidates.definition: Organizers deliberately create a common time and space (conferences, symposia, office redesigns) for encounters, removing some search costs of finding partners, while who meets whom remains unplanned.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes an organized event or designed space that brought them into contact with someone new, where the specific contact was not planned.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Purely informal, unstructured chance meetings (hallways, watercoolers), which the authors contrast with structured conference encounters.

candidates.label: Focused vs informal encounters
candidates.definition: Conference encounters differ from informal serendipitous encounters in hallways or at watercoolers because they focus the topic of knowledge sharing and idea exchange.
candidates.applies_when: The account notes that a chance meeting happened in a setting organized around a specific topic, which shaped what was discussed.

candidates.label: Exposure to someone's presentation
candidates.definition: Happening to hear another's presentation of their work sparks recognition that one could contribute to it.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes by chance attending a talk or poster and realizing their own capabilities could improve the presenter's work.

candidates.label: Approaching and following up
candidates.definition: The person acts on the encounter, approaching the other after the talk, and the conversation evolves into a collaboration.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes initiating contact after a chance exposure and the conversation developing into joint work.

candidates.label: Discovering complementarities
candidates.definition: Encounters let diverse partners exchange information, build intellectual links and discover potential complementarities they offer each other.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes realizing during an encounter that their skills or knowledge fit with the other's.

candidates.label: Repeated interaction to build relationship
candidates.definition: Developing an initial encounter into a multiplex, productive relationship requires time and repeated interactions.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes further meetings and sustained contact after the first encounter before joint output emerged.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: A one-off exchange with no subsequent relationship.

candidates.label: Common knowledge to make sense
candidates.definition: An encounter is effective only if people share enough common knowledge to understand each other's specialized knowledge and connect it to what they already know.
candidates.applies_when: The person mentions shared background, training or interests that let them grasp the value of what the other offered.

candidates.label: Field similarity
candidates.definition: Overlap in educational background, skills and training; aids early-stage collaborations but same-field partners may become competitive.
candidates.applies_when: The account references sharing (or not) the same discipline or professional training with the person met.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Overlap in personal research interests or passions, which is intellectual similarity.

candidates.label: Intellectual similarity
candidates.definition: Overlap in personal interests, passions and pursuits, which can span fields; moderate overlap aided learning from encounters.
candidates.applies_when: The person notes shared topical interests or passions with the encounter partner, possibly across different fields.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Shared formal discipline or training (field similarity).

candidates.label: Moderate similarity sweet spot
candidates.definition: Encounters are most productive when partners share some but not too much overlap; too little overlap prevents absorption, too much offers few novel ideas.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes the partner as different enough to bring new ideas yet similar enough to communicate easily.

candidates.label: High overlap breeds competition
candidates.definition: When partners have highly overlapping interests, encounters can reveal similar projects, heightening competition, a need to differentiate and withholding of recognition.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes meeting someone doing very similar work and reacting with rivalry, differentiation or reluctance to credit them.

candidates.label: Search costs and frictions
candidates.definition: Search costs and information frictions normally constrain whom people collaborate with; serendipitous encounters lower these costs.
candidates.applies_when: The account notes that without the encounter they would not have known about or found the partner.

candidates.label: Collaboration costs and matching
candidates.definition: Turning encounters into joint work is costly, requiring coordinated effort, aligned incentives, trust, creative synergy and compatibility of personality and schedules.
candidates.applies_when: The person discusses hurdles like aligning incentives, trust, personalities or schedules after meeting someone.

candidates.label: Proximity and incentives
candidates.definition: Geographic proximity increases the likelihood of serendipitous encounters, and incentives like grant funding can draw people into encounter settings.
candidates.applies_when: The account cites being nearby or attracted by funding/incentives to the setting where the encounter occurred.

candidates.label: Starting new collaborations
candidates.definition: Serendipitous encounters can spark new collaborations, as in the three-lab collaboration that arose from a chance conference talk.
candidates.applies_when: A new partnership or joint project is traced to a chance encounter.

candidates.label: Redirecting trajectories
candidates.definition: Encounters can reshape people's research directions, steering them toward the event's topic and broadening their networks.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes changing direction or focus after an encounter.

candidates.label: Learning and integrating outside work
candidates.definition: Encounters let people learn about outside work and integrate it into their own subsequent work.
candidates.applies_when: The account reports adopting ideas, methods or concepts learned from the encounter partner.

candidates.label: Slow, delayed payoff
candidates.definition: Results from encounters may emerge slowly, only after years, and short-term frictions are harder to overcome than long-term ones.
candidates.applies_when: The person notes that benefits from a chance meeting appeared long after it happened.

candidates.label: Homophily and prior ties
candidates.definition: Collaborations may instead form through preference for similar others or persistence of prior ties, not chance encounters.
candidates.applies_when: The partnership is explained by pre-existing relationships or seeking out similar others rather than an unexpected meeting.
